questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile platform attack vectors OWASP mobile top 10
questions.text: Which OWASP Mobile Top 10 category specifically covers vulnerabilities where an app stores sensitive data — such as credentials, API keys, or PII — in unprotected locations like Android SharedPreferences or iOS NSUserDefaults?

answers.text: M2: Insecure Data Storage
M1: Improper Platform Usage
M3: Insecure Communication
M5: Insufficient Cryptography

explanations.a: OWASP Mobile Top 10 M2 (Insecure Data Storage) covers vulnerabilities where apps store sensitive data in insecure locations — including Android's SharedPreferences (XML files readable by any root process), NSUserDefaults (iOS plist files), SQLite databases without encryption, device logs, and external storage. Attackers who root/jailbreak the device or use forensic tools can extract this data trivially.
explanations.b: M1 (Improper Platform Usage) covers misuse of a platform feature or failure to use platform security controls correctly — for example, misusing Android Intents, iOS keychain access controls, or biometric authentication APIs. It addresses how the app uses the OS features, not where it stores data.
explanations.c: M3 (Insecure Communication) covers weaknesses in network communication — unencrypted HTTP, improper TLS certificate validation, missing certificate pinning, and cleartext transmission of sensitive data over any network protocol.
explanations.d: M5 (Insufficient Cryptography) covers flaws in how apps implement cryptography — using broken algorithms (MD5, DES), weak key generation, hard-coded keys, or custom cryptographic implementations. It is about the quality of crypto used, not about storage location choices.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile platform attack vectors OWASP mobile top 10
questions.text: A mobile banking app transmits authentication tokens in HTTP request headers without TLS, allowing any party monitoring the network to capture them. Which OWASP Mobile Top 10 category does this vulnerability fall under?

answers.text: M2: Insecure Data Storage — the token is stored insecurely in transit
M3: Insecure Communication — sensitive data transmitted without adequate transport security
M7: Client Code Quality — the developer used an insecure HTTP library function
M9: Reverse Engineering — attackers can extract the token format from the binary

explanations.a: M2 addresses insecure storage of data on the device's local filesystem or memory. Transmission over a network — even if the data is later stored at the destination — is a communication issue, not a local storage issue. The vulnerability occurs during transit over the network.
explanations.b: OWASP Mobile M3 (Insecure Communication) directly covers this scenario: any transmission of sensitive data (authentication tokens, credentials, PII) over unencrypted channels (HTTP instead of HTTPS), with improper TLS configuration, or without certificate validation. Transmitting tokens in plain HTTP exposes them to passive sniffing on the same network (coffee shop Wi-Fi, rogue AP, ISP surveillance).
explanations.c: M7 (Client Code Quality) covers code-level issues like buffer overflows, format string vulnerabilities, and insecure use of third-party libraries that affect the app's robustness and memory safety. Using HTTP instead of HTTPS is an architectural and configuration decision, not a code quality bug in the narrow sense.
explanations.d: M9 (Reverse Engineering) covers the ability of attackers to decompile and analyze the app's binary to understand its logic, extract secrets, or find vulnerabilities. An attacker doesn't need to reverse engineer the app to capture plaintext network traffic — they simply monitor the network.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile platform attack vectors OWASP mobile top 10
questions.text: A mobile banking app relies exclusively on OS-level certificate validation for TLS and does not implement certificate pinning. Which specific attack does this omission enable that certificate pinning would prevent?

answers.text: SQL injection through the mobile API endpoint bypassing server-side input validation
Reverse engineering of the app's business logic by decompiling the APK with jadx
Man-in-the-middle interception of TLS traffic using a proxy with a CA certificate trusted by the device OS
Privilege escalation on rooted devices that access the app's internal storage directory

explanations.a: SQL injection targets server-side database queries — it is not related to certificate pinning or TLS validation. Certificate pinning specifically addresses the trustworthiness of the TLS server the app connects to, not the server's handling of input data.
explanations.b: Reverse engineering targets the app binary on the device — decompiling the APK/IPA to read source code logic. Certificate pinning does not affect the reversibility of the binary. Protections against reverse engineering include code obfuscation and anti-tampering checks.
explanations.c: Without certificate pinning, the app accepts any TLS certificate that chains to a trusted CA. If an attacker or tester installs a custom CA on the test device (e.g., Burp Suite's CA) and runs a proxy, the app trusts the proxy's certificate. The proxy decrypts, inspects, and re-encrypts all HTTPS traffic. Certificate pinning prevents this by requiring the server's certificate to match a specific hardcoded value, rejecting any certificate — even one from a trusted CA — that doesn't match.
explanations.d: Privilege escalation to access internal storage is a device-level rooting attack — it does not depend on certificate pinning. Even with certificate pinning enabled, a rooted device with direct filesystem access can read the app's data directory. Certificate pinning protects network communications, not local file access.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile platform attack vectors OWASP mobile top 10
questions.text: During an iOS app security assessment, a tester finds that OAuth2 access tokens are stored in the iOS Keychain using the kSecAttrAccessibleAlways accessibility attribute. Why is this a security concern compared to using kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly?

answers.text: The iOS Keychain is not encrypted — kSecAttrAccessibleAlways items are stored in plaintext accessible to any installed app
OAuth2 tokens stored with kSecAttrAccessibleAlways are automatically shared with all apps signed by the same developer Team ID
kSecAttrAccessibleAlways causes tokens to expire immediately when the device screen locks, breaking the user session

kSecAttrAccessibleAlways allows keychain item access even when the device is locked — a stolen device, forensic extraction tool, or malware active during device lock can access the tokens without the user's passcode

explanations.a: The iOS Keychain IS encrypted — it uses AES-256 encryption tied to hardware keys in the Secure Enclave. The accessibility attribute determines WHEN the decryption key is available, not whether encryption exists. All keychain items are encrypted; the attribute controls access timing.
explanations.b: Keychain items are sandboxed per app by default — different apps cannot access each other's keychain items unless an explicit Keychain Access Group is configured for sharing. kSecAttrAccessibleAlways does not create cross-app sharing between developer team apps automatically.
explanations.c: kSecAttrAccessibleAlways means items are accessible at ALL times, including when locked — it does not cause expiration. The concern is the opposite: tokens remain accessible even when they should be protected behind the device lock screen.
explanations.d: kSecAttrAccessibleAlways (or kSecAttrAccessibleAlwaysThisDeviceOnly) makes keychain items available without requiring the device passcode or biometric authentication. This means a forensic tool (like Cellebrite or GrayKey) can extract these tokens even from a locked device if it can exploit an iOS vulnerability to access the keychain. kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly restricts access to times when the device has been unlocked since last boot — significantly reducing the window of exposure. Sensitive tokens should use the most restrictive accessibility attribute consistent with the app's UX requirements.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: hacking android OS rooting ADB exploitation
questions.text: What is Android Debug Bridge (ADB), and why is it a security risk when enabled on a mobile device?

answers.text: ADB is a command-line communication tool for Android devices; when USB debugging is enabled, it allows anyone with physical USB access to install apps, extract data, and run shell commands without the device passcode
ADB is Android's built-in antivirus engine that blocks malicious app installation from unknown sources
ADB is the Android Backup Daemon that encrypts and uploads device backups to Google Drive automatically
ADB is a code-signing utility that verifies APK integrity before installation on Android devices

explanations.a: Android Debug Bridge (ADB) is a developer tool included in the Android SDK that provides a command-line interface to communicate with connected Android devices via USB or TCP/IP. When USB debugging is enabled (Developer Options), an attacker with physical access can use ADB to install APKs, extract files, execute shell commands, capture screenshots, dump memory, and create full device backups — all without needing the device's PIN, pattern, or password. This is a significant risk for unlocked devices or devices that are left unattended.
explanations.b: ADB has no antivirus or malware detection functionality. Android's Play Protect (in Google-licensed devices) and third-party security apps provide malware scanning — these are completely separate from ADB.
explanations.c: ADB does provide backup functionality via 'adb backup', but it is not a daemon and does not automatically upload to Google Drive. Google's automatic backup is a separate system service. ADB is an interactive developer tool, not an automated background service.
explanations.d: APK code signing is performed during app development using Android's apksigner tool and Java's jarsigner. ADB does not sign or verify APK signatures — it transfers and installs APKs. The Android package manager (pm) performs signature verification during installation.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: hacking android OS rooting ADB exploitation
questions.text: An attacker gains temporary physical access to an Android device with USB debugging enabled and the screen unlocked. Which ADB command creates a full backup of all installed apps and their data — including credentials potentially stored in SharedPreferences or SQLite databases?

answers.text: adb install malicious.apk — installs a malicious app silently on the target device
adb backup -all -apk -f device_backup.ab — creates a backup archive of all apps and their associated data
adb shell pm list packages -f — lists all installed app package names and their APK file paths
adb logcat -d > logfile.txt — dumps the Android system log buffer to a file on the attacker's computer

explanations.a: adb install installs an APK file from the attacker's computer to the target device. While malicious app installation is a real ADB attack vector, it does not extract existing app data or stored credentials from the device.
explanations.b: adb backup -all -apk -f device_backup.ab creates a compressed backup archive containing all apps' data (with -all) and their APK files (with -apk). The resulting .ab file can be converted to a .tar archive using Android Backup Extractor, then explored to find SharedPreferences XML files, SQLite databases, saved tokens, and other sensitive app data — all in a single command without needing to root the device.
explanations.c: adb shell pm list packages lists installed package names and paths, providing useful reconnaissance but not extracting any app data or credentials. This is an enumeration command, not a data extraction command.
explanations.d: adb logcat dumps the Android logcat (system log) buffer — useful for finding credentials accidentally logged by apps using Log.d() or Log.e() during development, but it only captures recent log entries, not persistent app data stored in databases or preferences files.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: hacking android OS rooting ADB exploitation
questions.text: What is the PRIMARY security risk of a rooted Android device in an enterprise environment managing sensitive corporate data?

answers.text: Rooted Android devices automatically broadcast their IMEI and device serial to nearby Bluetooth devices
Rooting permanently disables Android's GPS and location services, preventing MDM tracking
Rooting bypasses Android's application sandbox and SELinux MAC enforcement, allowing any root-privileged process to access other apps' private data, modify system files, and disable security controls
Rooted devices cannot connect to enterprise Wi-Fi networks configured with WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X) authentication

explanations.a: Rooting does not cause IMEI or serial number broadcasting via Bluetooth — IMEI is transmitted by the cellular modem during network registration, not via Bluetooth advertisements. This is a fabricated consequence with no basis in Android's architecture.
explanations.b: Rooting may affect some system services but does not permanently disable GPS. GPS hardware functionality is independent of the Android OS privilege model. MDM tracking using GPS can still function on rooted devices unless the MDM app itself is removed.
explanations.c: Android's security model relies on application sandboxing (each app runs as a separate Linux user ID, isolating its files) and SELinux MAC (Mandatory Access Control) policies that restrict what each process can access. When a device is rooted, the root user (UID 0) can access any file on the filesystem regardless of app sandbox boundaries, modify system files, disable SELinux enforcement (setenforce 0), intercept network traffic, extract keystore keys, and bypass MDM controls by accessing MDM app data directly. Any malicious app that requests root access gains full control over all device data.
explanations.d: WPA2-Enterprise (802.1X) authentication depends on EAP credentials or certificates — it does not check whether the device is rooted. A rooted device with valid certificates or credentials can authenticate to 802.1X networks normally. MDM compliance policies (not the Wi-Fi infrastructure) are used to detect rooted devices and deny resource access.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: hacking android OS rooting ADB exploitation
questions.text: A malicious Android app targets devices running Android 9. It exploits a buffer overflow in the media parsing library (mediaserver process) to achieve code execution, then uses a separate Linux kernel CVE to escalate from the media server's limited privilege to root. Which attack technique does this chain represent?

answers.text: A social engineering attack that manipulates the user into granting root permissions through a fake system dialog
An ADB-based exploit chain requiring physical USB access and enabled developer options
A supply chain attack that inserted malicious code into the official Google Play build pipeline
An exploit chain combining remote code execution via a media parsing vulnerability with a local privilege escalation CVE to achieve full device root compromise

explanations.a: Social engineering manipulates users psychologically — it does not involve chaining technical vulnerabilities. The described attack involves no user interaction beyond opening a malicious media file; it exploits memory safety bugs, not human psychology.
explanations.b: ADB-based attacks require physical USB access and developer options. The described attack operates entirely over the media parsing pathway (e.g., a malicious video or image opened in a media app) — no USB connection or ADB is involved. It is a fully remote or drive-by exploitation scenario.
explanations.c: A supply chain attack compromises the software development or distribution process — inserting malicious code into the build pipeline before distribution. The described attack targets an already-distributed device at runtime, exploiting existing vulnerabilities in shipped code — not the build process.
explanations.d: This describes a two-stage exploit chain: Stage 1 — RCE (Remote Code Execution): the buffer overflow in the media parsing library (running as the 'media' user with limited Android permissions) provides code execution but only in the sandboxed media server context. Stage 2 — LPE (Local Privilege Escalation): a separate kernel vulnerability is exploited from within the compromised media process, breaking out of the sandbox to gain root. This technique mirrors historical Android compromises (e.g., Stagefright variants) and is categorized as a Privilege Escalation via Exploit Chain in MITRE ATT&CK Mobile (T1404).

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: What is iOS jailbreaking, and which primary security boundary does it remove?

answers.text: Jailbreaking exploits iOS kernel vulnerabilities to disable Apple's code-signing enforcement and app sandbox restrictions, enabling installation of unsigned apps and unrestricted system-level access outside Apple's controls
Jailbreaking is Apple's official carrier unlock process that removes SIM restrictions for international travel
Jailbreaking is a factory reset procedure that removes unwanted pre-installed system applications
Jailbreaking is the MDM enrollment process that bypasses Apple's Device Enrollment Program for BYOD devices

explanations.a: iOS jailbreaking exploits vulnerabilities in the iOS kernel (and sometimes the bootchain) to: (1) remove Apple's code-signing enforcement (allowing unsigned and modified apps to run), (2) disable sandbox restrictions (allowing apps to access other apps' data and system files), (3) grant users root access, and (4) enable installation of apps from outside the App Store (via Cydia or Sileo). From a security perspective, jailbreaking eliminates the foundational iOS security model — attackers who jailbreak a device (or target an already-jailbroken device) have full control over all app data and system functions.
explanations.b: Carrier unlocking removes the SIM-lock restriction that limits a phone to a specific carrier's network. This is a separate, legitimate process offered by carriers — it does not modify the iOS kernel or security model and is unrelated to jailbreaking.
explanations.c: Factory reset (Settings > General > Reset > Erase All Content and Settings) restores iOS to its factory state by erasing all user data and returning the OS to stock configuration. This is a built-in Apple feature — it does not remove any system apps or modify iOS security boundaries.
explanations.d: Apple Device Enrollment Program (DEP/ADE) is an MDM enrollment mechanism for corporate device management. Bypassing DEP enrollment restrictions is a separate topic from jailbreaking — jailbreaking is about removing OS-level security restrictions, not MDM enrollment protocols.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: An iOS penetration tester uses Frida on a jailbroken test device to dynamically instrument a banking app, hooking its SSL validation function to bypass certificate pinning. Which app-level control would detect Frida's presence and terminate the app before testing can proceed?

answers.text: Compiling the app with Bitcode enabled, which prevents Frida from hooking Swift or Objective-C functions
Implementing jailbreak detection and anti-tampering checks that detect Frida's dylib injection, anomalous memory regions, or unexpected loaded libraries and terminate the process
Using AES-256-GCM encryption for all local data storage, which blocks Frida from reading plaintext values in memory
Validating the app's own TLS certificate chain to ensure Frida cannot intercept API calls

explanations.a: Bitcode is an intermediate representation Apple uses for App Store distribution optimization — it enables Apple to re-optimize apps for new hardware. Bitcode has no effect on Frida's ability to hook functions in a running process. Frida operates at the process memory level, not at the compilation artifact level.
explanations.b: Anti-jailbreak and anti-tampering controls can detect Frida by checking for: the presence of Frida's gadget dylib (frida-gadget.dylib) in the loaded library list (via dyld_image_count and dyld_get_image_name), anomalous memory regions associated with Frida's agent, suspicious environment variables or files Frida uses (/usr/lib/frida, /tmp/frida-*), or unexpected changes to function pointers. When detected, the app can terminate or wipe its memory. Note: determined attackers can bypass these checks, but they raise the bar significantly.
explanations.c: AES-256-GCM encryption protects data at rest in files. Frida operates in process memory space — even encrypted data is decrypted by the app before use, and Frida hooks functions after decryption occurs. Encrypting storage does not prevent Frida from reading in-memory plaintext values.
explanations.d: TLS certificate chain validation (or pinning) prevents MITM attacks on network traffic — it does not detect Frida's process-level instrumentation. Frida can bypass pinning by hooking the SSL validation function regardless of whether the app validates its own certificate. Anti-Frida checks and certificate pinning are complementary but independent controls.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: An attacker with a jailbroken iPhone installs SSL Kill Switch 2 from Cydia, which disables iOS certificate pinning checks system-wide. They then configure Burp Suite as a proxy on their laptop. What attack capability does this combination provide against a target financial app?

answers.text: Remote code execution in the financial app's process by injecting a malicious dylib through the proxy connection
Extraction of the app's compiled source code by transmitting the binary through the Burp proxy
Man-in-the-middle inspection of all decrypted HTTPS traffic — including authentication tokens, session cookies, account data, and API request/response content
Privilege escalation to iOS kernel level by exploiting entitlements declared in the app's provisioning profile

explanations.a: Remote code execution via a proxy connection is not how Burp Suite or SSL Kill Switch 2 operate. These tools intercept HTTP/HTTPS traffic — they do not inject executable code into the target app's process. Code injection requires different techniques (Frida, cycript, LLDB).
explanations.b: Burp Suite is an HTTP proxy — it cannot extract or transmit compiled binary code from the app. The app's IPA binary would need to be pulled from the device filesystem using SSH or ADB, not captured through an HTTP proxy.
explanations.c: With certificate pinning disabled by SSL Kill Switch 2, the financial app no longer verifies that the TLS server certificate matches its hardcoded pin — it accepts any certificate trusted by the OS. Installing Burp's CA on the device (or trusting it system-wide on a jailbroken device) causes the app to trust Burp's proxy certificate. Burp then decrypts all HTTPS sessions, exposing authentication tokens, session cookies, account numbers, transaction data, and API endpoints in plaintext for inspection and manipulation.
explanations.d: iOS entitlements are declared in the app's provisioning profile and enforced by the kernel's Secure Enclave — they define what system capabilities the app can access. SSL Kill Switch 2 does not modify entitlements or provide kernel-level privileges. Jailbreaking itself bypasses kernel security, but SSL Kill Switch specifically targets SSL pinning, not privilege escalation.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: An iOS app assessor uses the 'strings' command and rabin2 to extract readable content from an iOS app binary and discovers a hardcoded third-party API key. Which OWASP Mobile category applies, and what is the MOST secure architectural remediation?

answers.text: M3 (Insecure Communication) — fix by rotating the API key after each use within the app
M6 (Insecure Authorization) — fix by validating the key's permission scope server-side on each API call
M7 (Client Code Quality) — fix by enabling Bitcode compilation to prevent string extraction from the binary

M8 (Code Tampering) / M9 (Reverse Engineering) — fix by never embedding secrets in the binary; retrieve them at runtime from an authenticated server-side secrets vault, requiring valid user authentication before issuing the key

explanations.a: M3 addresses insecure network communication — it is about how data travels between the app and servers, not about secrets embedded in the binary. Rotating an API key after each use would not prevent extraction from the binary if the initial key is still hardcoded.
explanations.b: M6 (Insecure Authorization) addresses broken or missing access control checks in the app or on the server. Server-side validation of the key's scope is a good practice but does not address the fundamental problem that the key is hardcoded in an app that millions of users download — anyone who extracts it can make authorized API calls as if they were the app.
explanations.c: M7 (Client Code Quality) covers memory safety bugs, format string vulnerabilities, and insecure third-party library usage — not secrets management in the binary. Bitcode compilation does not prevent string extraction — rabin2 and strings operate on the device-installed binary after any Apple-side optimization, not on Bitcode IR.
explanations.d: Hardcoding secrets in a mobile binary violates OWASP M8 (Code Tampering protection — secrets can be extracted) and M9 (Reverse Engineering). The secure architectural pattern is: (1) never embed secrets in the binary, (2) authenticate the user first (username/password, biometric, OAuth), (3) after authentication, retrieve the API key or token from a server-side secrets vault (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) via an authenticated API call, (4) use the key in memory only for the session duration. This ensures that extracting the binary yields no usable secrets.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile device management MDM policies enrollment
questions.text: Which MDM enrollment model allows employees to use their personal devices for work while maintaining a technical separation between corporate apps/data and personal content, typically using containerization technology?

answers.text: Apple DEP / Android Zero Touch — fully corporate-manages the device from factory enrollment
BYOD enrollment with containerization — corporate apps are isolated in a managed container while personal data remains separate and private
Corporate-owned personally enabled (COPE) — company owns the device but allows personal use
Certificate-based enrollment — uses PKI client certificates to authenticate devices to the MDM server

explanations.a: Apple DEP (Device Enrollment Program) and Android Zero Touch are automated enrollment mechanisms for corporate-owned devices that provide full MDM control from initial device setup. These approaches give IT complete management over the entire device — they are not used for employee-owned (BYOD) personal devices where privacy separation is required.
explanations.b: BYOD (Bring Your Own Device) enrollment with containerization (e.g., Samsung Knox, Microsoft Intune with Android Work Profile, or Apple Managed Open-In) creates a secure corporate container on the employee's personal device. Corporate apps, email, and data reside in the managed container (encrypted separately, under IT control), while personal apps and data remain outside IT's reach. IT can wipe the corporate container without affecting personal photos, messages, or apps.
explanations.c: COPE (Corporate-Owned, Personally Enabled) is a deployment model where the company provides and owns the device but allows employees to also use it for personal purposes. The company maintains full MDM control. This is different from BYOD where the employee owns the device.
explanations.d: Certificate-based enrollment is a technical authentication method for the MDM enrollment process itself — it describes HOW a device authenticates to the MDM server (using a client certificate), not the overall deployment model defining device ownership and data separation policies.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile device management MDM policies enrollment
questions.text: An employee reports their MDM-enrolled corporate smartphone stolen. IT needs to protect sensitive corporate email and documents on the device immediately. Which MDM capability provides the MOST appropriate response for a BYOD device?

answers.text: Remotely rotate the corporate Wi-Fi password to prevent the finder from connecting to internal networks
Disable the device's cellular connection via MDM to prevent the finder from making calls or using data
Issue a selective remote wipe command that erases only the corporate container and its data while preserving the employee's personal photos, messages, and apps
Activate the device's camera remotely to photograph the person currently in possession of the device

explanations.a: Rotating the Wi-Fi password prevents devices from connecting to that specific Wi-Fi network going forward — but the stolen device likely already had cached credentials and can use cellular data. Additionally, this action affects all employees who need to reconnect to the Wi-Fi. It does not protect data already on the stolen device.
explanations.b: MDM solutions do not typically have the capability to disable cellular connectivity on iOS or Android devices remotely. Cellular communication is controlled by the device's baseband processor and SIM card, not by MDM profiles. Some carriers can deactivate a SIM upon request, but this is a carrier-level action, not an MDM command.
explanations.c: Selective remote wipe (also called corporate wipe or selective wipe) is the appropriate response for BYOD devices. It erases only the MDM-managed container — deleting corporate email, apps, documents, certificates, and VPN configurations — while leaving all personal content (photos, personal apps, personal accounts) intact. This balances data security with the employee's privacy rights and avoids destroying personal data on a device the employee owns.
explanations.d: Remotely activating a device's camera is not a standard MDM capability in legitimate enterprise MDM solutions (Intune, Jamf, VMware Workspace ONE). This would violate privacy laws and user trust. MDM capabilities are defined by the device's MDM profile and are strictly controlled by Apple and Google to prevent MDM abuse.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile device management MDM policies enrollment
questions.text: An MDM policy mandates a minimum 6-digit passcode and 5-minute auto-lock on all enrolled iOS devices. An employee disables their passcode for convenience. What action does MDM compliance enforcement MOST likely trigger automatically?

answers.text: MDM immediately issues a full device wipe to protect all corporate data on the non-compliant device
MDM sends a push notification politely requesting the employee re-enable their passcode within 24 hours
MDM remotely re-enables the passcode on the device without notifying the user or requiring their input
MDM marks the device non-compliant and automatically blocks its access to corporate resources (email, VPN, SharePoint) until the passcode is restored

explanations.a: A full device wipe for removing a passcode would be a massively disproportionate response and would destroy employee data on a BYOD device. MDM compliance policies escalate remediation in stages — access restriction is the standard first response, not immediate data destruction.
explanations.b: Notification-only responses are a gentle approach but do not provide immediate protection. Most enterprise MDM solutions (Intune Conditional Access, Jamf Pro Smart Groups) enforce compliance automatically without waiting for the user to respond to a notification. Notification may also be sent alongside access restriction, but it is not the primary enforcement mechanism.
explanations.c: iOS does not allow MDM solutions to remotely set or override device passcodes — Apple's MDM protocol does not include this capability for privacy and security reasons. MDM can enforce passcode requirements and block access for non-compliance, but it cannot forcibly set a passcode that the user doesn't know.
explanations.d: MDM compliance enforcement (via Conditional Access policies in Microsoft Intune/Azure AD, or equivalent in other MDM platforms) evaluates device compliance status in real time. When the passcode is removed, the device is marked non-compliant, and Conditional Access policies block authentication tokens for corporate resources — preventing access to Exchange Online email, SharePoint, VPN, and other integrated applications until the device returns to compliance.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile device management MDM policies enrollment
questions.text: An organization uses Apple Business Manager with Automated Device Enrollment (ADE). A tester discovers that the MDM enrollment process authenticates devices using the device serial number only, without a cryptographic device attestation challenge. Which attack does this design weakness enable?

answers.text: An attacker who obtains a target device's serial number could provision a different physical device through the enrollment process, receiving corporate MDM profiles and VPN credentials intended for the legitimate device
Attackers can download all corporate MDM configuration profiles by submitting arbitrary SCEP enrollment requests to the MDM server
The ADE enrollment workflow is vulnerable to MITM because all device-to-MDM communications use unencrypted HTTP
Serial number-based enrollment allows completely unenrolled devices to access corporate resources by replaying enrollment completion certificates

explanations.a: Apple ADE (formerly DEP) assigns device serial numbers to MDM servers in Business Manager. During enrollment, the device contacts Apple's servers with its serial number to receive the MDM server URL, then contacts the MDM server to download the enrollment profile. If the MDM server relies solely on the serial number for device identity (without requiring cryptographic proof that the device is the genuine hardware with that serial — e.g., via Apple's Device Identity Attestation), a sophisticated attacker who knows the serial number could potentially spoof the enrollment and receive corporate profiles including VPN configurations, certificates, and Wi-Fi credentials. Apple introduced Managed Device Attestation to address this using the Secure Enclave to cryptographically prove device identity.
explanations.b: SCEP (Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol) requires challenge passwords or one-time tokens for enrollment — it is not susceptible to arbitrary enrollment by serial number submission alone. SCEP enrollment requires pre-shared enrollment credentials issued by the MDM administrator.
explanations.c: ADE device-to-Apple and device-to-MDM communications use HTTPS/TLS — they are not transmitted in cleartext HTTP. Apple's MDM protocol requires TLS for all MDM communications. The vulnerability in the question is about device authentication identity, not transport security.
explanations.d: MDM enrollment completion certificates (MDM push certificates) are device-specific and cryptographically tied to the enrolled device's identity. Replaying enrollment certificates from one device on a different device would fail because the MDM server tracks device identity through the certificate's public key, which is device-specific.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: Which OWASP standard provides a comprehensive security requirements framework for mobile applications, organized into tiered levels (L1 Standard, L2 Defense-in-Depth, L3 Resilience) covering data storage, authentication, cryptography, network communication, and platform interaction?

answers.text: CIS Mobile Device Security Benchmark
OWASP Mobile Application Security Verification Standard (MASVS)
NIST Mobile Threat Catalogue (NIST IR 8144)
PCI DSS Mobile Payment Acceptance Security Guidelines

explanations.a: The CIS Mobile Device Security Benchmarks provide configuration hardening guidelines for mobile device operating systems (Android, iOS) — they cover OS-level settings and MDM configurations for enterprise device management. They do not provide mobile application security requirements for developers.
explanations.b: OWASP MASVS (Mobile Application Security Verification Standard) defines security requirements for mobile app developers and security testers in three levels: L1 (standard security, required for all apps), L2 (defense-in-depth requiring additional controls for sensitive apps like banking), and R (resilience requirements for apps needing protection against reverse engineering). Its companion guide, the OWASP MASTG (Mobile Application Security Testing Guide), provides detailed testing procedures for each MASVS requirement.
explanations.c: NIST IR 8144 (Mobile Threat Catalogue) provides a structured taxonomy of mobile threats organized by threat category and technical impact. It is a reference document for threat modeling — not a security verification standard defining specific app security requirements.
explanations.d: PCI DSS Mobile Payment Acceptance Security Guidelines provide security requirements specifically for payment acceptance applications (card readers, mPOS solutions). They are narrowly focused on payment card security and do not cover general mobile app security domains like authentication, cryptography, or platform interaction.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: A mobile security assessor uses MobSF (Mobile Security Framework) during initial triage of an Android APK before manual testing. Which specific combination of capabilities makes MobSF particularly valuable for this early phase?

answers.text: MobSF can perform live exploitation of discovered vulnerabilities on production apps running on real devices in the field
MobSF downloads apps directly from the Google Play Store API without requiring the assessor to obtain the APK file separately

MobSF performs automated static analysis (decompiling the APK, scanning for hardcoded secrets, insecure APIs, exported components) and dynamic analysis (running the app in an emulator and monitoring behavior), generating a consolidated security report
MobSF cracks Android Keystore encryption to extract hardware-backed credentials during dynamic analysis sessions

explanations.a: MobSF is a security analysis tool — it identifies vulnerabilities but does not exploit them on production apps. Exploitation is the responsibility of the human assessor who uses MobSF's findings to plan manual test cases. MobSF operates in controlled testing environments, not against production deployments.
explanations.b: MobSF does not have a Google Play Store API integration to download apps directly. The assessor must provide the APK (Android) or IPA (iOS) file directly to MobSF for analysis. APKs can be obtained through various means (device extraction, third-party APK sites for testing, or direct developer builds).
explanations.c: MobSF provides both static and dynamic analysis capabilities: Static analysis decompiles the APK using jadx, analyzes the AndroidManifest.xml for exported components and dangerous permissions, scans for hardcoded secrets (API keys, passwords), detects insecure API usage, and checks for known vulnerable library versions. Dynamic analysis runs the app in an Android emulator, monitors HTTP/HTTPS traffic, logs file system operations, and captures system API calls. The combined report provides immediate triage without requiring fully manual analysis from scratch.
explanations.d: Android Keystore hardware-backed keys (backed by the Secure Enclave or TEE) cannot be extracted by any software tool — they are designed to be non-exportable at the hardware level. MobSF has no capability to break hardware security modules or extract TEE-protected key material.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: A security assessor uses Drozer during an Android security assessment. Which specific testing capability does Drozer provide that static APK analysis with jadx or apktool cannot?

answers.text: Drozer decompiles and de-obfuscates ProGuard-protected Android APK bytecode for source code review
Drozer analyzes Android network traffic as a transparent HTTP/HTTPS proxy between the app and its backend
Drozer performs GPU-accelerated brute-force attacks against encrypted Android SQLite database files

Drozer interacts with live running Android IPC components — testing exported Activities, ContentProviders, Services, and BroadcastReceivers for unauthorized access, data leakage, and privilege escalation at runtime

explanations.a: Decompiling ProGuard-obfuscated code is the function of tools like jadx (decompiler), smali/baksmali (bytecode assembler/disassembler), and apktool (APK unpacker). Drozer is a dynamic testing framework — it does not perform static decompilation or de-obfuscation of APK bytecode.
explanations.b: HTTP/HTTPS proxy functionality for Android app traffic is provided by Burp Suite (with its Android certificate installed) or mitmproxy. Drozer communicates with the Android device through its own agent app installed on the device and interacts with app components — it is not a network proxy.
explanations.c: Brute-forcing SQLite encryption is performed by tools like sqlitebrowser (for unencrypted), SQLCipher-aware brute-force tools, or hashcat. Drozer does not perform cryptographic attacks against database encryption.
explanations.d: Drozer is the industry-standard tool for testing Android IPC (Inter-Process Communication) attack surfaces. Using Drozer's agent installed on the device, a tester can: enumerate all exported app components (dz> run app.package.attacksurface), query ContentProviders directly without being the intended app (dz> run app.provider.query), send malicious Intents to exported Activities or Services, and test for path traversal in content URI handling. This dynamic, runtime testing reveals vulnerabilities that static analysis alone cannot confirm because IPC behavior depends on runtime conditions.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: A Drozer assessment reveals an Android app's ContentProvider is exported without permission enforcement, allowing any installed app to query all user records. Which remediation MOST effectively restricts access to only the app's own components while allowing legitimate internal use?

answers.text: Define a custom permission in AndroidManifest.xml with android:protectionLevel='signature', declare it on the ContentProvider's readPermission/writePermission attributes, and enforce it in the provider's query/insert/update/delete methods
Move all data from the ContentProvider to SharedPreferences, which is inaccessible to external apps without root access
Enable certificate pinning in the ContentProvider to authenticate callers before serving any data
Set android:debuggable='false' in the manifest, which prevents external ContentProvider access in release builds

explanations.a: Signature-level permissions (android:protectionLevel='signature') are only grantable to apps signed with the same certificate as the app defining the permission — effectively restricting access to components within the same developer's signing key. By declaring the permission on the ContentProvider using android:readPermission and android:writePermission, and calling checkCallingPermission() within the provider methods, only apps signed by the same developer (i.e., the app's own components running in a different process, or explicitly trusted partner apps) can access the provider. This is the recommended Android pattern for protecting inter-app IPC components.
explanations.b: SharedPreferences stores data in XML files within the app's private data directory (/data/data/packagename/shared_prefs/). While external apps cannot directly access these files without root (unlike an exported ContentProvider), moving data to SharedPreferences eliminates the ContentProvider's functionality entirely. If the ContentProvider exists to share data between app components or with trusted partner apps, replacing it with SharedPreferences breaks this design. The correct fix is proper permission enforcement, not data store migration.
explanations.c: Certificate pinning is a TLS network security mechanism — it validates the TLS certificate of a network server. ContentProvider interactions are local IPC calls within Android — they do not use TLS certificates and have no concept of network-level certificate authentication. Certificate pinning has no applicability to ContentProvider access control.
explanations.d: android:debuggable='false' prevents ADB shell access and debug bridge attachment in release builds. It does not affect ContentProvider access control — ContentProvider export and permission settings control inter-app access regardless of the debuggable flag. An exported ContentProvider without permissions is accessible from any installed app whether debuggable is true or false.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: Which mobile threat category silently monitors a device owner's calls, messages, GPS location, and app usage without their knowledge, is typically installed by an abuser or controlling employer, and is often marketed as 'parental control' or 'employee monitoring' software?

answers.text: Adware — displays intrusive advertisements within mobile applications and browsers
Stalkerware (commercial spyware) — covertly collects and exfiltrates personal device activity to a remote operator
Mobile ransomware — encrypts device storage or locks the screen and demands cryptocurrency payment
Scareware — displays false security alerts to frighten users into paying for fake mobile antivirus subscriptions

explanations.a: Adware displays unwanted advertisements — pop-ups, interstitials, banner ads — within apps or browsers. While intrusive and potentially privacy-invasive (tracking ad interests), adware's primary purpose is advertising revenue, not covert personal surveillance. Adware typically does not intercept calls, messages, or location data without the user's awareness.
explanations.b: Stalkerware (also called commercial spyware or intimate partner surveillance software) is intentionally designed to be invisible to the device owner. Once installed (typically by someone with physical access to the device), it silently logs call records, reads SMS and messaging app content, tracks GPS location, captures screenshots or keystrokes, and uploads all data to a remote control panel accessible to the installer. Products like mSpy, FlexiSPY, and Hoverwatch fall into this category. Cybersecurity organizations including the Coalition Against Stalkerware actively combat this threat.
explanations.c: Mobile ransomware locks the device screen or encrypts files and demands payment — typically cryptocurrency — for restoration. Unlike stalkerware, ransomware is immediately visible to the victim (the lock screen or ransom note is the attack's mechanism). It does not silently monitor device activity.
explanations.d: Scareware presents false security alerts claiming the device is infected or has detected viruses, pressuring users to pay for fake 'antivirus' apps. Like ransomware, scareware is overt — its effectiveness depends on the user seeing the alert. It does not involve covert surveillance.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: An Android device exhibits unusual battery drain, elevated cellular data usage, and the user notices an unknown system app with microphone and location permissions. Which investigation step MOST directly confirms whether spyware is present?

answers.text: Perform an immediate factory reset to remove the suspected spyware without further forensic analysis
Check the device's IMEI number against a stolen device registry to determine if the device was reported stolen
Enumerate installed packages with ADB or a security tool to identify suspicious apps with excessive permissions, and analyze network traffic logs for C2 communications to known spyware infrastructure
Replace the device's SIM card at the carrier store to prevent call interception from continuing

explanations.a: Immediate factory reset removes evidence along with the malware — it destroys forensic artifacts needed to confirm spyware presence, identify the specific software, document the data exfiltrated, or support legal proceedings against the person who installed it. Resetting should only be done after forensic preservation if possible.
explanations.b: IMEI registry checks identify whether a device was reported stolen — they have no bearing on whether software surveillance is running on the device. The IMEI check cannot detect installed apps or network behavior.
explanations.c: Systematic investigation for spyware includes: (1) ADB shell pm list packages -f (enumerate installed packages including hidden/system apps) to find unknown packages, (2) comparing installed packages against known stalkerware IOCs databases (KasperskyTIP, NCSC lists), (3) using network traffic analysis (Wireshark, PCAPdroid on-device capture, or router logs) to identify outbound connections to known spyware C2 domains or IP ranges, and (4) reviewing app permission grants via Settings > Privacy > Permission Manager for over-privileged unknown apps. Tools like Amnesty Tech's MVT can analyze Android backup files for stalkerware IOCs.
explanations.d: SIM card replacement changes the device's cellular identity (phone number, IMSI) — it does not remove installed software from the device. Stalkerware operates through the installed app on the device, not through the SIM card. A new SIM would not stop spyware that monitors local device activity, uses the camera, or captures screen content — it would only change the cellular carrier data routing.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: Pegasus spyware (NSO Group) exploited zero-click vulnerabilities in iMessage and other iOS attack surfaces to compromise iPhones with no user interaction. Which characteristic makes zero-click delivery fundamentally harder to defend against than traditional phishing-based mobile malware?

answers.text: Pegasus was delivered exclusively through Android sideloading, completely bypassing App Store security review
Pegasus required the victim to jailbreak their device before the spyware installation process could begin
Pegasus was factory-installed by device manufacturers as part of a hardware supply chain compromise

Zero-click vulnerabilities trigger without any user action — clicking a link, opening an attachment, or tapping a notification is not required — making user awareness training completely ineffective as a defense

explanations.a: Pegasus targeted iPhones (iOS), not Android. Sideloading on iOS requires jailbreaking or enterprise provisioning profiles — Pegasus used zero-click exploits in standard iOS components (iMessage, FaceTime, Apple Music) to compromise devices without any sideloading. Android was a secondary target.
explanations.b: Pegasus specifically exploited non-jailbroken iPhones — compromising them silently without any device modification by the victim. One of its most notable capabilities was achieving kernel-level code execution on fully patched iOS devices with no visible indication to the user or any need for the victim to take action.
explanations.c: Pegasus is software-based spyware delivered over the air through iOS exploit chains — not hardware supply chain compromise. Supply chain attacks involve tampering during manufacturing or distribution; Pegasus operates through remote software exploitation of running devices.
explanations.d: Traditional mobile phishing (malicious links, fake app installs, malicious attachments) requires the victim to take an action — tap a link, install an app, open a file. Security awareness training can reduce these risks. Zero-click exploits trigger purely by receiving a specially crafted message (iMessage, WhatsApp, GIF) — the attack fires without the victim reading, opening, or interacting with the message in any way. This completely bypasses behavioral defenses, making patching (eliminating the underlying vulnerability) the only effective mitigation.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: A mobile forensics examiner suspects a non-jailbroken iPhone belongs to a journalist targeted with sophisticated spyware. Standard visual inspection reveals nothing unusual. Which detection methodology is MOST likely to surface evidence of advanced mobile spyware on a non-jailbroken iOS device?

answers.text: Analyze iOS system diagnostic logs and network traffic captured from the iPhone using Amnesty International's Mobile Verification Toolkit (MVT) to search for known IOCs and anomalous process indicators
Install a reputable antivirus app from the App Store that scans all installed apps for spyware signatures in real time
Visually inspect Settings > Privacy & Security to identify any unauthorized permission grants for microphone, camera, or location
Restore the device from the most recent iCloud backup and check if the suspicious behavior persists after restoration

explanations.a: Amnesty International Security Lab's MVT (Mobile Verification Toolkit) was developed specifically for this use case — detecting advanced spyware (including Pegasus) on iOS devices. MVT analyzes: iTunes/iMazing backup contents, iOS filesystem acquisitions (from jailbroken devices or AFC2 pairing), network traffic PCAP files, and diagnostic logs. It searches for known IOCs including spyware-associated domain names in network connections, suspicious process names in crash logs, anomalous library injections, and database entries left by spyware frameworks. MVT identified Pegasus infections that had no visible indicators on a standard inspection.
explanations.b: App Store antivirus apps on iOS operate under strict sandbox restrictions — they cannot scan other apps' processes, access system files, or monitor kernel-level activity. Apple's iOS sandboxing specifically prevents the kind of deep system access that spyware detection requires. App Store security apps can check Safari browsing safety and offer phishing link protection but cannot detect sophisticated spyware that operates at the system or kernel level.
explanations.c: Visual inspection of permission settings shows current permission grants but cannot detect spyware that: uses legitimate-looking app names, operates with permissions that appear granted by a legitimate app, or exploits kernel vulnerabilities to access sensors without going through the permission system. Advanced spyware specifically evades visual inspection.
explanations.d: Restoring from iCloud backup may re-install spyware if the backup was taken after the infection occurred — it would not clean a compromised device. Additionally, sophisticated spyware (like Pegasus) may persist across backups if the compromise is at a deep enough system level. Restoration destroys forensic evidence without necessarily confirming or removing the spyware.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile network attacks SS7 rogue BTS
questions.text: Which telecommunications signaling protocol, designed in 1975 for inter-carrier routing with no built-in authentication or encryption, is exploited by attackers to intercept SMS messages — including SMS-based two-factor authentication codes — and track mobile subscribers' locations worldwide?

answers.text: LTE (4G Long-Term Evolution) — the modern cellular data and voice protocol
DIAMETER — the authentication and authorization protocol used in 4G/LTE core networks
SS7 (Signaling System No. 7) — the legacy inter-carrier signaling protocol with no inherent authentication
SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) — the VoIP call setup and teardown protocol used by internet telephony

explanations.a: LTE is the 4G standard for cellular data and VoLTE (Voice over LTE) and includes improved security compared to earlier generations. While LTE networks have their own vulnerabilities (4G IMSI catchers, diameter protocol attacks), LTE itself is not SS7 and was designed with authentication improvements over 2G/3G systems.
explanations.b: DIAMETER replaced SS7's RADIUS for AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) in 4G networks. While DIAMETER has its own security issues and can be targeted in 4G networks, SS7 is the older protocol used for inter-carrier signaling that lacks authentication entirely.
explanations.c: SS7 (ITU-T Q.700 series) was designed in 1975 as a closed, trust-based system for routing calls and SMS between telephone carriers. All carriers on the SS7 network were implicitly trusted — no authentication was required because access was physically controlled by carrier infrastructure. As SS7 access became available to more parties (MVNOs, roaming partners, SS7 gateways), malicious actors gained access and exploited this trust model to intercept SMS, reroute calls, and track subscriber location via MAP (Mobile Application Part) messages — particularly SendRoutingInfoForSM and ProvideSubscriberInfo.
explanations.d: SIP is the protocol used by VoIP systems (IP phones, softphones, internet calling services) for establishing, maintaining, and terminating voice/video calls over IP networks. SIP has its own security concerns (SIP replay attacks, toll fraud) but is not related to SS7 inter-carrier signaling or SMS interception at the cellular network level.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile network attacks SS7 rogue BTS
questions.text: An attacker with access to an SS7 network sends a SendRoutingInfoForSM (SRI-SM) MAP message targeting a victim's phone number, and the network returns the victim's IMSI and the MSC address. What follow-on attack does this information enable?

answers.text: Remotely wiping the victim's SIM card by sending an over-the-air firmware update via the SS7 MAP stack
Cloning the victim's SIM card by extracting the Ki authentication key from the MSC response
Launching a denial-of-service attack against the victim's MSC by flooding it with fake MAP signaling
Re-routing SMS messages intended for the victim through the attacker's network element, intercepting 2FA codes and password reset links

explanations.a: SS7 MAP messages cannot remotely wipe SIM cards or deliver firmware updates to subscriber devices. SIM OTA (Over-The-Air) updates are sent via SMS using a separate ETSI specification (TS 102.226) and require the operator's OTA key infrastructure — they are not triggered by SS7 MAP SRI-SM queries.
explanations.b: The Ki (authentication key) is stored securely in the SIM card and in the HLR/AuC — it is never transmitted in network signaling. An MSC address response does not contain the Ki. SIM cloning attacks that steal Ki require physical access to the SIM card (for legacy SIMs) or HLR database compromise, not SS7 interception.
explanations.c: A denial-of-service via MAP flooding is theoretically possible but is not the primary attack enabled by obtaining the IMSI and MSC address from a SRI-SM query. The attacker's goal in this attack chain is interception, not disruption.
explanations.d: With the victim's IMSI and serving MSC address, the attacker sends a RegisterSMS (SRI-SM or UpdateLocation) MAP message to the victim's HLR, registering a fake MSC/VLR under the attacker's control as the subscriber's current location. Subsequent SMS messages destined for the victim are routed to the attacker's fake MSC, which delivers them to the attacker rather than the legitimate device. This is how SS7 attacks intercept 2FA SMS codes — a devastating attack against SMS-based authentication. This attack chain was publicly demonstrated in 2014 (German researchers) and subsequently exploited in real-world bank account hijacking attacks.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile network attacks SS7 rogue BTS
questions.text: A rogue base station (IMSI catcher / Stingray) is positioned near a target building, broadcasting a stronger signal than legitimate cell towers. Nearby 2G (GSM) phones automatically connect to it. Which attack does this enable that is specific to 2G's authentication model?

answers.text: Active MITM — the rogue BTS authenticates the device to itself, but GSM's authentication is one-way (network does not authenticate to the device), allowing the rogue BTS to strip encryption or downgrade to A5/0 (no encryption)
Passive recording of LTE traffic for offline decryption using the rogue BTS's supercomputer
Physical cloning of the device's eSIM profile by reading SIM toolkit commands over-the-air
Bluetooth credential theft by exploiting the proximity connection between GSM's cellular stack and the phone's BLE chipset

explanations.a: GSM (2G) has a critical design flaw: authentication is one-way — the network authenticates the device (using the SIM's Ki to respond to a challenge), but the device cannot authenticate the network. A rogue BTS can pass the authentication challenge to the legitimate network (relaying it), pass the response back, and then man-in-the-middle all subsequent communication. Additionally, the rogue BTS controls the encryption negotiation — in GSM, it can instruct the device to use A5/0 (no encryption) or the weak A5/2 cipher, and many GSM phones comply without user warning. This allows plaintext capture of voice calls and SMS messages.
explanations.b: LTE traffic requires the LTE encryption keys specific to each session — a passive recording cannot be decrypted without them. Additionally, LTE implements mutual authentication (the device authenticates the network as well as the network authenticating the device), which prevents simple IMSI catcher attacks without more sophisticated techniques.
explanations.c: eSIM cloning requires access to the SM-DP+ provisioning server and operator authentication credentials. Physical GSM proximity via an IMSI catcher does not provide access to eSIM provisioning infrastructure or SIM toolkit commands that would enable cloning.
explanations.d: GSM cellular protocols and Bluetooth Low Energy operate on completely separate radio stacks. Proximity through an IMSI catcher creates a cellular connection — it does not create a Bluetooth pairing and provides no access to the BLE chipset or its protocols.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.keyword: mobile network attacks SS7 rogue BTS
questions.text: A corporate security team wants to detect when employee smartphones near the office connect to rogue base stations (IMSI catchers). Which observable indicator on the device is MOST reliably associated with IMSI catcher activity?

answers.text: Elevated battery consumption indicating unusual RF transmission power from the device

Unexpected downgrade from 4G/LTE to 2G (GSM) in an area with confirmed full LTE coverage, which reverts to LTE after toggling Airplane Mode — a pattern consistent with IMSI catcher forced network downgrade
Undelivered SMS messages that appear as sent in the outbox but not received by the intended recipients
The device IMEI number displaying differently between the phone dialer (*#06#) and the SIM tray label

explanations.a: IMSI catchers can cause elevated battery drain (the device may try to reconnect to legitimate towers or maintain connections to both the rogue and legitimate cells), but battery drain alone is a non-specific indicator with many innocent causes (background app activity, poor signal area, aging battery). It is not reliable as a primary IMSI catcher indicator.
explanations.b: IMSI catchers typically operate as 2G (GSM) base stations because 2G's one-way authentication allows the rogue BTS to act as MITM without the device detecting network illegitimacy. To force modern 4G-capable phones to connect, the IMSI catcher may broadcast jamming signals on LTE frequencies or exploit LTE security gaps to force a 2G fallback. Observing a sudden unexplained 2G downgrade in a location with established LTE coverage — especially one that resolves when Airplane Mode is cycled to force a fresh cell selection — is a meaningful indicator of potential IMSI catcher presence. Apps like AIMSICD and SnoopSnitch monitor for this and other indicators.
explanations.c: Undelivered SMS messages could result from many causes: recipient phone off, full inbox, network congestion, or carrier routing issues. While SS7-based SMS interception does divert messages, the device sending the message typically receives a delivery report and would not show 'sent but not delivered' in a way distinguishable from normal delivery failure.
explanations.d: The IMEI is burned into the device's baseband firmware and does not change between reboots, calls, or SIM tray checks. IMEI inconsistency between *#06# and the label would indicate hardware tampering or a counterfeit device — not IMSI catcher activity.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: Which IoT messaging protocol uses a publish-subscribe model with a central broker, is designed for high-latency and low-bandwidth environments, and is widely used for sensor data collection in smart home, industrial, and agricultural IoT deployments?

answers.text: HTTP/REST — the standard stateless request-response protocol used in cloud IoT APIs
CoAP (Constrained Application Protocol) — UDP-based REST-like protocol for resource-constrained devices
MQTT (Message Queuing Telemetry Transport) — lightweight publish-subscribe protocol over TCP for IoT data
AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) — enterprise-grade reliable messaging protocol for financial systems

explanations.a: HTTP/REST is used in cloud-connected IoT platforms and device management APIs, but it is a request-response protocol requiring a persistent connection for each request. HTTP's overhead (headers, full TCP connection setup) makes it inefficient for battery-constrained sensors sending frequent small telemetry updates.
explanations.b: CoAP (RFC 7252) is a lightweight protocol designed specifically for constrained IoT devices (microcontrollers, sensors), running over UDP for reduced overhead. CoAP mirrors REST principles (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and supports multicast. While excellent for constrained environments, CoAP uses a request-response model, not publish-subscribe with a broker.
explanations.c: MQTT (originally developed by IBM and Arcom in 1999, standardized as OASIS MQTT) uses a broker-based publish-subscribe model: publishers send messages to topics on the broker, and subscribers receive messages for topics they subscribe to — without publishers needing to know subscribers exist. MQTT over TCP is extremely lightweight (2-byte fixed header), supports QoS levels (0, 1, 2), and is well-suited for unreliable or high-latency links. It is the dominant IoT messaging protocol for telemetry collection.
explanations.d: AMQP (Advanced Message Queuing Protocol) is an enterprise message queuing protocol designed for high-reliability, transactional messaging between business systems (financial transactions, enterprise service buses). While technically capable of IoT use, its overhead and complexity make it unsuitable for constrained IoT sensors.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: An IoT smart home hub is discovered to have Telnet running on port 23 with hardcoded default credentials (admin/admin) that cannot be changed, and no firmware update mechanism. Which attack is MOST directly enabled by this combination of weaknesses?

answers.text: A MITM attack intercepting encrypted ZigBee frames between the hub and connected smart bulbs
A timing side-channel attack extracting the hub's AES key through power consumption analysis
A certificate pinning bypass enabling HTTPS interception of the hub's cloud API traffic
Remote unauthorized access via Telnet using the known default credentials, achieving persistent device control and network pivot capability

explanations.a: A ZigBee MITM attack targets the ZigBee mesh protocol (802.15.4) used for smart device communication — it is a wireless protocol-level attack requiring a ZigBee radio, not a Telnet connection. The hub's Telnet exposure is a separate, more direct attack surface.
explanations.b: Power analysis side-channel attacks require physical access to the device's power supply lines and specialized oscilloscope equipment. They target the cryptographic implementation on the hardware — they do not exploit Telnet credentials or network-level access.
explanations.c: Certificate pinning bypass attacks target HTTPS client implementations in apps — they require intercepting TLS traffic from the hub's cloud API client. This requires a network MITM position, not direct Telnet access. The hub's Telnet service provides a more direct attack vector.
explanations.d: Telnet transmits all data in plaintext (no encryption) and requires no prior network MITM — an attacker on the same network (or internet-exposed hub) simply connects to port 23 and enters admin/admin. With shell access, the attacker can: enumerate the network, modify hub configuration, install persistent backdoors, use the hub as a pivot point to attack other network-connected devices, and (given no firmware update mechanism) the vulnerability cannot be patched by the manufacturer.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: A security researcher discovers an MQTT broker exposed on the internet without TLS and with anonymous access enabled (no username/password required). After connecting, what data is the researcher MOST likely to observe in the subscribed topics?

answers.text: Plaintext sensor readings, GPS coordinates, device status messages, temperature values, and potentially control commands — all transmitted without any encryption or access control
AES-128 encrypted device telemetry protected by MQTT's built-in session key negotiation mechanism
Only MQTT protocol management messages — MQTT prevents payload data from being accessed by anonymous subscribers
Anonymized telemetry with personal identifiers removed per MQTT version 5's privacy-by-design specification

explanations.a: MQTT is designed for simplicity — when deployed without TLS and with anonymous access, all message payloads are transmitted in cleartext and accessible to any subscriber. Real-world exposed MQTT brokers (discoverable via Shodan) have been found publishing: home automation states (door lock/unlock events, occupancy), industrial sensor readings (temperature, pressure), vehicle GPS tracks, home security alarm states, and agricultural equipment status — often including personally identifiable location data and operational commands that could be replayed to control physical devices.
explanations.b: MQTT does not have built-in encryption or session key negotiation — it is a transport-agnostic protocol that relies on TLS at the transport layer for encryption. MQTT itself transmits payloads as raw bytes with no inherent confidentiality. Without TLS, there is no encryption regardless of MQTT version.
explanations.c: MQTT anonymous access (allow_anonymous true in Mosquitto configuration) grants the connecting client subscription access to all topics permitted by the ACL (access control list). Without ACL configuration, the default is typically unrestricted access to all topics. MQTT has no built-in mechanism to prevent anonymous subscribers from reading payload data.
explanations.d: MQTT version 5 introduced new features including user properties, reason codes, and topic aliases — it did not introduce privacy-by-design anonymization of payload data. MQTT is payload-agnostic; anonymization of sensor data is the responsibility of the application, not the MQTT protocol.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: An IoT deployment uses a single hardcoded symmetric AES-128 key embedded in all 10,000 sensor firmware images — used for both encrypting telemetry and authenticating device identity. A security architect identifies this as a critical design flaw. Why?

answers.text: Symmetric keys are mathematically unsuitable for device authentication — only asymmetric key pairs with X.509 certificates can verify device identity in IoT deployments

If any single device is physically compromised and its firmware is extracted, the shared key is recovered — enabling an attacker to decrypt all 10,000 devices' telemetry and impersonate any device in the fleet
The MQTT protocol specification prohibits sharing symmetric keys across devices — each device must use a unique key per the OASIS MQTT standard
Using the same key for both encryption and authentication violates AES-GCM's requirement for cryptographically independent keys for each operational mode

explanations.a: Symmetric keys can be used for device authentication through challenge-response schemes (HMAC-based: the server sends a nonce, the device HMACs it with the shared key, the server verifies). Symmetric authentication is technically feasible but is architecturally weaker than asymmetric because: (1) both parties must know the key, and (2) compromise of either party's key compromises the shared secret. The core problem stated is the shared key across all devices, not symmetric vs. asymmetric.
explanations.b: Sharing one key across 10,000 devices creates catastrophic blast radius from a single compromise. An attacker who physically opens one sensor (common for publicly accessible IoT hardware), reads the firmware from flash memory using JTAG or SPI bus sniffing, and extracts the hardcoded AES key now has: full decryption capability for all 10,000 devices' historical and future telemetry data, the ability to forge authentication from any device in the fleet, and persistent access that cannot be revoked without replacing all 10,000 firmware images. Best practice is unique per-device keys generated during secure manufacturing provisioning.
explanations.c: MQTT has no specification regarding key sharing between devices — it is a messaging protocol, not a key management standard. MQTT is agnostic to how applications implement security, and OASIS MQTT standards do not define key uniqueness requirements.
explanations.d: AES-GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) is an authenticated encryption mode that provides both confidentiality and integrity/authentication in a single operation. AES-GCM does not require different keys for encryption and authentication components — it uses one key for both (the same key generates the GHASH authentication tag and the CTR keystream). The problem with shared keys is not an AES-GCM violation.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: The Mirai botnet (2016) infected hundreds of thousands of IoT devices and launched record-breaking DDoS attacks. What was Mirai's PRIMARY method for compromising IoT devices at scale?

answers.text: Exploiting zero-day vulnerabilities in IoT device firmware update mechanisms over HTTPS
Conducting MITM attacks to intercept and manipulate IoT device provisioning traffic
Scanning the internet for IoT devices with Telnet or SSH open and trying a hardcoded list of 61 common default username/password pairs
Distributing trojanized firmware updates through compromised IoT vendor cloud update servers

explanations.a: Mirai's source code (leaked in 2016) shows it did not exploit firmware update zero-days. Its infection mechanism was credential brute-force, not vulnerability exploitation of complex update protocols. Zero-day exploitation is far more resource-intensive and would not have achieved the scale Mirai reached.
explanations.b: Mirai did not perform MITM attacks on provisioning traffic. It was a simple, mass-scale credential-brute-force worm that worked because millions of IoT devices (cameras, DVRs, routers) used factory-default credentials and had Telnet exposed to the internet.
explanations.c: Mirai contained a hardcoded list of 61 default credential pairs (e.g., admin/admin, root/root, root/1234) and continuously scanned random IP address ranges for Telnet (port 23) and other management services. When a device responded, Mirai tried all credential pairs. Successful logins triggered a command to download and execute the Mirai binary. This simple technique was devastatingly effective against the millions of unsecured consumer IoT devices connected to the internet.
explanations.d: Mirai did not target vendor update servers or distribute fake firmware updates. Its propagation was entirely network-based credential brute-force — no supply chain manipulation was involved.

questions.name: Mobile Platform, IoT, and OT Hacking
questions.text: A Mirai-infected IoT botnet receives a command to launch an attack by sending maximum-bandwidth UDP packets with spoofed source IP addresses to random destination ports on the target's IP address. Which DDoS technique does this describe?

answers.text: Slowloris — opening many partial HTTP connections to exhaust the target web server's connection threads
SYN flood — sending TCP SYN packets without completing handshakes to exhaust the target's connection state table
DNS amplification — sending small DNS queries with spoofed source IPs to open resolvers that amplify responses toward the target
UDP flood — overwhelming the target's bandwidth and processing capacity with high-volume spoofed UDP packets, forcing ICMP Destination Unreachable responses

explanations.a: Slowloris is an application-layer HTTP DoS attack that sends partial HTTP requests, keeping connections open indefinitely to exhaust the server's concurrent connection limit. It requires very little bandwidth from the attacker. Mirai's primary attacks were volumetric, not application-layer connection exhaustion.
explanations.b: SYN floods exploit TCP's three-way handshake — sending SYN packets without completing the handshake fills the server's SYN backlog (half-open connection queue) until it cannot accept new connections. SYN floods use TCP, not UDP, and target connection state, not bandwidth.
explanations.c: DNS amplification is a reflection/amplification attack where small DNS queries (with spoofed source IPs) are sent to open resolvers, which send large DNS responses (up to 70x larger) to the spoofed target IP. Mirai was known to use DNS amplification, but the described attack — UDP packets to random ports — is a direct UDP flood, not a DNS reflection.
explanations.d: UDP flood attacks send high volumes of UDP datagrams to random destination ports on the target. For each UDP packet received on a closed port, the target's OS sends an ICMP Destination Unreachable response — consuming CPU and bandwidth on both send and receive paths.
